description.en: The archer pull-up is an advanced pull-up variation where you pull up primarily with one arm while the other arm extends straight out to the side along the bar. It is the primary progression toward a one-arm pull-up, loading one side of the back much more heavily than a standard pull-up.

en: Hang from a pull-up bar with a very wide overhand grip — as wide as the bar allows.
Pull your body up while shifting toward your right hand, pulling primarily with your right arm.
As you rise, your left arm straightens out along the bar. At the top, your right arm is fully bent and your left arm is nearly straight.
Your chest should approach your right hand at the top. Squeeze your right lat hard.
Lower under control back to a full hang.
On the next rep, pull toward your left hand. Alternate sides or complete all reps on one side.
If this is too difficult, start with assisted archer pull-ups using a resistance band.
Aim for low reps (2 to 5 per side). Quality matters more than volume.
Primary progression toward a one-arm pull-up
Heavily loads one side of the back
Builds unilateral lat and bicep strength
Develops body control and coordination
Builds grip strength asymmetrically
Impressive advanced calisthenics skill

description.en: The assisted lying leg raise with lateral throw down is a partner driven core exercise. The partner pushes the legs to alternating sides instead of straight down, hammering the obliques eccentrically.

en: Lie flat on your back with the partner standing at your head.
Reach up and grasp the partner ankles for stability.
Brace the core and lift both legs straight up to vertical.
When the legs reach the top the partner pushes them to one side.
Resist the push and lower the legs slowly with control.
Stop just before the heels touch the floor on the side.
Lift the legs back up to the top with control.
Continue the leg raise and alternating side throws for all reps.
Hammers the obliques through eccentric throw downs.
Builds rotational core strength.
Trains the abs and hip flexors together.
Adds challenge beyond standard leg raises.
Develops anti rotation control.
Excellent finisher for serious ab work.

description.en: The band alternate lat pulldown with twist combines a unilateral lat pulldown with a torso twist. The lifter anchors a band overhead and pulls down with one arm while rotating the torso. The combo trains the lats and obliques in a strong functional pattern.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead to a sturdy point.
Stand or kneel below the anchor.
Grip the band with both hands overhead.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Pull one elbow down to the side rotating the torso toward that side.
Squeeze the lat and obliques at the bottom.
Return with control to the start.
Pull the other arm down with the opposite twist. Alternate sides.
Combo lat and rotation move
Trains rotational core
No machine needed
Builds the lats
Strong band combo
Useful at-home back move

description.en: The band one arm twisting seated row combines a unilateral seated row with a torso twist. The lifter sits with the band anchored in front, rows with one hand, and rotates the torso through the pull. The combo trains the lats and obliques together.

en: Anchor a resistance band low at chest height in front of you.
Sit on the floor with legs extended.
Grip the band with one hand at arms length.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Pull the band back rowing the elbow past the body.
At the same time twist the torso toward the working side.
Squeeze the lat and obliques at the top.
Untwist and return with control. Switch sides.
Combo back and rotation move
Trains rotational core
Strong unilateral back move
Builds the lats
Strong band combo
Useful core builder

description.en: The barbell box squat is a powerlifting squat variation where you sit your hips back to a box at the bottom of each squat, then explode back up. The box ensures consistent depth, teaches sitting back into the squat, and builds explosive concentric strength. Westside Barbell popularized it as a foundational training tool.

en: Place a sturdy box (or stack of plates) directly behind you at the appropriate squat depth — typically just below parallel.
Set a barbell at upper-back height in a power rack. Step under and place it across your upper traps. Unrack and step back.
Stand directly in front of the box with feet shoulder-width apart.
Sit your hips back as if reaching for the box. Continue lowering until your butt touches the box.
Pause completely on the box for one to two seconds. Do not collapse — maintain tension.
Drive through your full feet to explode back up to standing.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top.
Maintain perfect bar position and brace throughout.
Teaches consistent squat depth
Trains sitting back into the squat
Builds explosive concentric strength
Reduces stress on the knees
Foundational powerlifting variation
Builds posterior chain

description.en: The barbell hip thrust is a horizontal hip-extension exercise that loads the glutes through their strongest range. With your upper back supported on a bench and a loaded barbell across your hips, you drive your hips up to lockout and squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Research consistently ranks the hip thrust among the most effective exercises for glute development.

en: Sit on the floor with your upper back against the long edge of a bench. The bench should hit just below your shoulder blades.
Roll a loaded barbell over your legs until it sits in the crease of your hips. Use a barbell pad or folded towel for comfort.
Plant your feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart, with your shins close to vertical when your hips are at the top of the lift. Adjust your foot position so this is the case.
Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Drive through your heels and push your hips straight up.
At the top, your torso and thighs should form a straight line parallel to the floor. Squeeze your glutes hard for one second.
Lower your hips under control until they are just above the floor, then drive back up. Do not let the bar rest on the floor between reps.
Repeat for the desired number of reps, then carefully roll the bar off your hips.
Most effective exercise for isolating and overloading the glutes
Allows for very heavy loading once form is dialed in
Builds glute strength that carries over to squats, deadlifts, and sprinting
Easier on the lower back than other heavy hip-extension movements
Improves hip extension power for athletic performance

description.en: The barbell incline triceps extension skull crusher is a skull crusher performed on an incline bench. The bench angle pulls the elbows behind the head, biasing the long head of the triceps for greater stretch and growth. It is one of the best moves for triceps mass.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie back on the bench with feet flat on the floor.
Have a spotter pass you a barbell or pick it up off the floor.
Hold the bar with a shoulder-width grip with arms extended overhead.
Brace your core and keep your back against the bench.
Bend at the elbows to lower the bar behind your head.
Keep your upper arms still and only the elbows moving.
Extend the elbows to return to the start position.
Targets the triceps long head
Deep stretch on the triceps
Builds triceps mass
Strong hypertrophy move
Reduces shoulder strain
Useful for arm size

description.en: The Jefferson deadlift is an old-school lift where you straddle the barbell with one foot in front and one foot behind it, then lift the bar from between your legs. The asymmetric stance creates a unique loading pattern that builds the legs, hips, and core while reducing spinal compression compared to a conventional deadlift.

en: Stand over the loaded barbell with your feet straddling it — one foot in front of the bar, one foot behind, both feet flat.
The bar should run between your legs and roughly under your hips. Take a wider stance for stability.
Squat down and grip the bar with one hand in front of the body and one hand behind, palms facing you.
Brace your core, lift your chest, and engage your lats.
Drive through both feet to stand up tall, lifting the bar between your legs.
Lock out hips and knees at the top with the bar held in front of and behind your body.
Lower the bar back to the floor under control by reversing the motion.
Switch your stance halfway through your sets to balance left and right development.
Builds full-body strength with reduced spinal load
Hits glutes, quads, and adductors uniquely
Develops core anti-rotation strength
Strong grip and forearm work from the unusual hand position
Old-school lift that reveals weaknesses in stabilizers
Lower back-friendly compared to conventional deadlift

description.en: The barbell standing wide military press is performed with a wider than shoulder-width grip on the bar. The wide grip changes the elbow path and shifts emphasis from the front delts to the medial deltoids. The standing position builds total core and lower back stability under heavy load.

en: Set up a barbell at upper chest height in a power rack.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and step back into your stance.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and brace your core.
Squeeze your glutes to lock the hips.
Press the bar straight up overhead, moving your head forward as the bar passes.
Lock out at the top with the bar directly over your shoulders.
Lower the bar back to the front rack position with control.
Wide grip emphasizes medial delts
Builds shoulder width
Strong core and lower back stability work
Different stimulus than standard military press
Useful for breaking through shoulder plateaus
Builds total shoulder size

description.en: The bent arm shoulder stretch is a classic overhead tricep stretch where you raise one arm overhead, bend at the elbow, and reach your hand down behind your head. The opposite hand can gently pull the elbow further to deepen the stretch. It targets the triceps, lats, and shoulders.

en: Stand or sit tall. Reach your right arm straight up overhead.
Bend your right elbow to drop your right hand down behind your head, between your shoulder blades.
Reach your left hand up and grasp your right elbow.
Gently pull your right elbow toward the left, deepening the stretch.
Feel the stretch through the back of your right upper arm (tricep), right lat, and right shoulder.
Keep your chest lifted and core braced.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Switch sides and repeat.
Deeply stretches the triceps and shoulders
Opens the lats
Improves overhead mobility
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Excellent post-workout stretch for arm and pressing days

description.en: The bodyweight standing pulse calf raise is a calf builder that uses small partial pulses at the top of the range. The lifter raises onto the toes, then performs short up and down pulses to keep tension on the calves. It is a strong burnout style move.

en: Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Set the toes pointing straight ahead.
Brace your core and keep the legs straight.
Press up onto the balls of the feet.
Hold near the top of the calf raise.
Lower a few inches and press back up in small pulses.
Keep the pulses short and controlled.
Continue until the calves fatigue.
Builds the calves
High time under tension
No equipment needed
Strong burnout move
Useful calf finisher
Trains calf endurance

description.en: The bodyweight windmill performs the windmill movement with no external weight — one arm extended overhead and the other reaching toward the floor as you hinge laterally at the hips. It builds lateral hip mobility, oblique strength, and shoulder stability without load.

en: Stand with feet wider than hip-width. Turn your left foot out 45 degrees.
Extend your right arm straight overhead.
Push your right hip out to the right.
Hinge to the left — slide your left hand down your left leg toward the floor.
Keep your right arm overhead. Look up at your right hand.
Continue until your left hand touches the floor (or as low as flexibility allows).
Drive your right hip forward to stand back up.
Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per side.
Builds lateral hip mobility
Develops oblique strength unloaded
Teaches the windmill pattern before loading
No equipment needed
Improves hamstring flexibility
Excellent warm-up for loaded windmills

description.en: The bottle weighted alternate hammer curl uses weighted water bottles for an alternating hammer curl pattern. The neutral grip targets the brachialis and brachioradialis along with the biceps. It is a strong at-home arm builder when no dumbbells are available.

en: Stand tall holding a weighted bottle in each hand at the sides.
Grip the bottles with a neutral palm facing the body.
Set the elbows tight against the sides.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Curl one bottle up toward the shoulder with palms facing in.
Squeeze the brachialis hard at the top.
Lower the bottle back down with control.
Repeat on the other side. Continue alternating arms.
Strong at-home arm builder
Trains the brachialis
Builds forearm thickness
No dumbbells required
Useful arm builder
Travel-friendly setup

description.en: The bridge pose Setu Bandhasana is a foundational yoga back bend. The mover lies on the back and lifts the hips while keeping the shoulders grounded. It opens the chest, strengthens the glutes, and stretches the hip flexors.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Place the heels close to the glutes.
Set the arms at the sides palms down.
Brace your core and inhale to prepare.
Press through the heels to lift the hips up.
Roll the shoulders under and clasp the hands beneath.
Lift the chest up toward the chin.
Hold the pose then release with control.
Opens the chest
Stretches the hip flexors
Strong yoga pose
Useful for back health
Builds the glutes

description.en: The cable glute dominant step up uses a low cable attached to a belt or held in front of the body during a step up. The forward lean and cable resistance shift emphasis to the glutes and hamstrings instead of the quads. It is a great loaded glute builder.

en: Attach a low cable to a belt around your waist (or hold a handle at your chest).
Stand facing away from the cable in front of a sturdy box.
Step forward to add tension to the cable.
Place one foot fully on the box.
Lean your torso forward over the working leg.
Drive through the heel of the working foot to step up onto the box.
Squeeze the glute hard at the top.
Step back down with control. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Glute-focused step up
Constant cable tension
Builds single-leg glute strength
Reduces quad dominance
Useful for glute hypertrophy
Improves hip extension power

description.en: The cable incline pushdown is a tricep pushdown variation performed lying on an incline bench facing a high cable. The incline position changes the resistance angle, loading the tricep through a different path than standing pushdowns and emphasizing the long head more.

en: Set an incline bench (30 to 45 degrees) facing away from a high cable. Attach a straight bar or rope.
Lie face up on the incline bench. Grip the bar overhead.
Start with elbows bent, bar behind your head.
Push the bar forward and down by extending at the elbows.
Lock out in front of your chest. Squeeze your triceps.
Slowly let the bar return behind your head.
Keep upper arms still.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Different resistance angle than standing pushdowns
Emphasizes the tricep long head
Constant cable tension
Incline position prevents cheating
Easy to load progressively
Useful for tricep hypertrophy

description.en: The cable seated supine grip row uses an underhand (supinated) grip on a straight bar attachment during a seated cable row. The supinated grip shifts the elbow path tight to the body, increasing lat engagement and adding strong bicep involvement. It is a classic variation for lat thickness training.

en: Sit at a low cable row station with a straight bar attached.
Brace your feet on the platform with knees slightly bent.
Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing up.
Sit tall with chest up and arms extended forward.
Brace your core.
Pull the bar to your lower abdomen by driving the elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze the lats and biceps at the back of the row.
Slowly extend the arms forward to the starting position with control.
Supinated grip emphasizes lats
Strong bicep involvement
Builds lat thickness
Different stimulus than overhand grip rows
Constant cable tension
Useful for lat and bicep training

description.en: The cow stretch (Cow Pose or Bitilasana) is a yoga warm-up performed on hands and knees where you arch your back, drop your belly, and lift your head and tailbone toward the ceiling. It mobilizes the spine into extension and is the counterpart to the cat stretch. Together they form the cat-cow flow — one of the best spinal warm-ups.

en: Start on your hands and knees in a tabletop position. Hands under shoulders, knees under hips, spine neutral.
Inhale and drop your belly toward the floor while lifting your tailbone and head toward the ceiling.
Arch your back gently. Open your chest forward.
Look up slightly without crunching your neck.
Feel the stretch across your front body and the gentle compression in your lower back.
Hold for one breath, then exhale and round your back into Cat Pose.
Continue alternating between cow and cat for 8 to 12 cycles.
Move with your breath — inhale into cow, exhale into cat.
Mobilizes the spine into extension
Warms up the entire back gently
Combined with cat pose, creates spinal flexion-extension flow
Calming and meditative
No equipment needed
Foundational yoga warm-up

description.en: The decline shoulder tap is a plank shoulder tap with the feet elevated on a box or bench. The decline angle adds more upper body load and increases the anti-rotation challenge while one hand taps the opposite shoulder. It is a strong core and shoulder builder.

en: Place your feet on a sturdy box or bench.
Set your hands flat on the floor under your shoulders.
Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line.
Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips stable.
Lift one hand off the floor and tap the opposite shoulder.
Hold the tap briefly without letting the hips rotate.
Plant the hand back down and repeat with the other hand.
Continue alternating taps with control.
Brutal anti-rotation challenge
Builds shoulder stability
Trains core control
Strong loaded plank variation
No special equipment needed
Useful for athletes

description.en: The diamond push-up (also called a close-grip or triangle push-up) is a push-up variation where you place your hands close together beneath your chest, forming a diamond shape with your thumbs and index fingers. The narrow hand position dramatically shifts emphasis from the chest to the triceps, making it the single most effective bodyweight tricep exercise.

en: Get into a high-plank position on the floor. Place your hands directly under your chest, touching your thumbs and index fingers together to form a diamond (or triangle) shape.
Step your feet back so your body forms a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your hips level.
Lower your chest toward your hands by bending at the elbows. Keep your elbows tucked tight against your body — do not let them flare.
Lower until your chest touches or nearly touches your hands.
Press back up by extending at the elbows, driving your hands into the floor. Focus on squeezing your triceps throughout.
Lock out at the top with arms fully extended.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. If these are too difficult, use an incline surface to reduce the load.
The most effective bodyweight tricep exercise
Heavily loads the triceps with no equipment
Also builds the inner chest and anterior deltoid
Trains core stability through the plank position
Works anywhere — no equipment needed
Easy to scale by adjusting surface angle

description.en: The dumbbell overhead squat holds one or two dumbbells locked out overhead while performing a full-depth squat. It demands exceptional shoulder mobility, core stability, and ankle flexibility. It is used as a mobility assessment and an accessory exercise for Olympic lifting.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Press two dumbbells overhead with arms locked out.
Position the dumbbells slightly behind your head. Arms should be in line with your ears.
Brace your core hard. Keep your chest tall.
Sit your hips back and down into a full squat while keeping the dumbbells locked overhead.
Descend as deep as your mobility allows — ideally below parallel.
Keep your torso upright. The dumbbells should stay directly over your midfoot.
Drive through your full foot to stand back up while maintaining the overhead position.
Use light weight — this exercise prioritizes mobility over load.
Demands exceptional shoulder mobility
Builds core stability under overhead load
Improves squat depth and ankle flexibility
Useful mobility assessment tool
Accessory exercise for Olympic lifting
Exposes mobility weaknesses

description.en: The dumbbell RDL to jump shrug is a power combo where each Romanian deadlift transitions into an explosive jump shrug at the top. It trains the entire posterior chain, develops hip extension power, and builds traps in one movement. It is a strong choice for athletes needing more vertical pop.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Hinge at the hips and lower the dumbbells along your shins.
Stop when you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings.
Drive through the floor and explosively extend your hips.
As you stand tall, shrug your shoulders forcefully and rise up onto the balls of your feet.
Allow a small jump or hop at full extension.
Land softly with knees slightly bent.
Reset and begin the next rep with a controlled hinge.
Trains hip extension power
Builds the full posterior chain
Develops trap mass and power
Improves vertical jump
Useful for athletic training
Combines strength and explosive work

description.en: The EZ barbell decline close grip face press is a triceps focused pressing variation performed on a decline bench. The close grip and decline angle shift the load onto the triceps long head while the upper chest assists.

en: Lie back on a decline bench and secure your feet under the foot pads.
Hold an EZ curl bar with a close pronated grip and press it up over your chest.
Brace your core and keep your shoulder blades pinned to the bench.
Lower the bar slowly toward your forehead by bending the elbows.
Keep the elbows tracking forward and slightly tucked through the descent.
Stop when the bar nearly reaches your forehead without touching it.
Press the bar back up in a smooth arc by extending the elbows fully.
Pause briefly at the top and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Hammers the long head of the triceps under a deep stretch.
Builds size and strength in the triceps for stronger pressing lockouts.
Engages the upper chest and front deltoids as supporting movers.
EZ bar grip is wrist friendly compared to a straight bar.
Decline angle keeps tension on the triceps throughout the lift.
Improves elbow extension control for compound press variations.

description.en: The ez barbell reverse grip curl is a reverse curl using an ez bar. The lifter grips the bar with palms facing down (pronated) and curls. The pronated grip biases the brachioradialis and forearms over the biceps. It is a strong forearm builder.

en: Stand tall holding an ez curl bar with a pronated overhand grip.
Set the hands on the outer curves of the bar.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Set the elbows tight against the sides.
Curl the bar up toward the chest by bending the elbows.
Keep the elbows fixed at the sides throughout.
Squeeze the brachioradialis hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Strong forearm builder
Trains the brachialis
Builds forearm thickness
Easy on the wrists
Useful arm builder
Strong ez bar move

description.en: Front lever reps (front lever raises) hang from a bar and raise the body from a dead hang to the horizontal front lever position, then lower back down. Unlike the static front lever hold, this version performs dynamic reps for lat and core strength.

en: Hang from a bar with straight arms.
Engage your lats and core. Raise your body toward horizontal (front lever position).
Continue until your body is as close to horizontal as your strength allows.
Lower under control back to the dead hang.
Continue for reps.
Start with tucked front lever raises and progress to full.
This is extremely demanding — 3 to 5 reps is an accomplishment.
Progressions: tuck → advanced tuck → straddle → full.
Builds dynamic front lever strength
Develops lat power through the raising motion
Harder than static front lever holds
Advanced calisthenics exercise
Builds extraordinary core and back strength
Progressive with tuck variations

description.en: The glute march holds a glute bridge position and alternately lifts one foot off the floor while maintaining the bridge. It builds glute activation, single-leg hip stability, and anti-rotation core strength.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Bridge your hips up.
Maintain the bridge position throughout.
Lift your right foot 2 to 4 inches off the floor. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds.
Return it to the floor.
Lift your left foot. Hold.
Continue alternating — marching in place from the bridge.
Keep your hips level — do not let them drop when one foot lifts.
Aim for 10 to 15 marches per side.
Builds glute activation and endurance
Develops single-leg hip stability
Anti-rotation core demand from alternating
Beginner-friendly
No equipment needed
Excellent warm-up for lower-body training

description.en: The hack one leg calf raise uses a hack squat machine to load single leg calf raises. The lifter sets up under the pads and performs calf raises one leg at a time. The machine support allows heavy unilateral calf training.

en: Set up in a hack squat machine with the pads on the shoulders.
Place one foot on the platform with the heel hanging off.
Lift the other leg off the platform.
Brace your core and keep the working leg straight.
Lower the heel below the platform for a stretch.
Press up onto the ball of the foot to a full calf raise.
Squeeze the calf hard at the top.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Loads single leg calf
Strong unilateral calf
Builds calf size
Trains each side
Useful machine variation
Builds the calves

description.en: The hamstring stretch is any of several positions used to lengthen the muscles on the back of the thigh. Tight hamstrings limit hip flexion, contribute to lower-back pain, and reduce performance in squats and deadlifts. The most common variations include the seated single-leg hamstring stretch, the standing hamstring stretch, and the lying (supine) hamstring stretch with a strap.

en: Seated single-leg hamstring stretch: Sit on the floor with one leg extended in front of you and the other foot tucked against your inner thigh. Hinge at the hips (not the lower back) and reach toward the toes of the extended leg. Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then switch sides.

Standing hamstring stretch: Place one heel on a low step or curb with the leg straight and toes pointing up. Hinge at the hips and lean your chest toward the extended leg until you feel a stretch along the back of the thigh. Keep your back flat. Hold for 20 to 30 seconds per side.

Lying hamstring stretch: Lie on your back and loop a strap or towel around the ball of one foot. Keep the other leg flat on the floor. Straighten the lifted leg toward the ceiling and gently pull it closer using the strap until you feel a stretch. Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then switch.
For all variations, the stretch should come from a hip hinge, not from rounding your spine. Breathe deeply and ease deeper into the stretch on each exhale.
Stretch daily for noticeable flexibility gains within a few weeks. Hamstrings respond well to consistent, frequent stretching.
Increases flexibility and range of motion at the hips
Reduces lower-back tension caused by tight hamstrings pulling on the pelvis
Improves squat depth, deadlift setup, and overall lifting mechanics
Reduces injury risk in running, sprinting, and field sports
Helps relieve sciatic-type discomfort when paired with glute and hip stretches

description.en: Hip thrusts are a glute-focused hip extension exercise performed by sitting with your upper back against a bench and thrusting your hips upward. The bench-supported position allows full glute contraction at the top — making it the most effective bodyweight glute exercise. It is the foundation for all weighted hip thrust variations.

en: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a flat bench. Your shoulder blades should rest on the bench edge.
Plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, roughly 12 to 18 inches in front of you.
Brace your core. Tuck your chin slightly. Keep your gaze forward.
Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor.
Continue until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your shoulders. Your shins should be roughly vertical at the top.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not hyperextend your lower back.
Lower under control back toward the floor. Touch lightly, then drive up again.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps. Progress to weighted variations once bodyweight becomes easy.
Most effective bodyweight glute exercise
Foundation for all weighted hip thrust variations
Builds glute size and strength with no equipment
Easier on the lower back than many glute exercises
Trains glute activation for squats and deadlifts
Easy to progress to weighted versions

description.en: The hollow hold is a foundational gymnastics and CrossFit core exercise where you lie on your back and hold a hollow body position — slightly rounded back, ribs down, legs and arms extended. It builds anterior core strength critical for advanced calisthenics and is the foundation for hollow rocks and many gymnastics skills.

en: Lie flat on your back. Press your lower back firmly into the floor.
Lift your shoulders, head, and legs slightly off the floor.
Reach your arms overhead alongside your ears. Keep legs straight and pointed.
Round your upper back slightly. Pull your ribs down toward your hips. This is the hollow position — your body forms a gentle banana shape.
Brace your core hard. Maintain this position rigidly.
Hold for as long as you can while maintaining perfect form (start with 15 to 30 seconds, build to 60+).
If your lower back lifts off the floor, regress by bending your knees (tuck hold) or lowering your arms.
Breathe steadily — do not hold your breath.
Foundational gymnastics core hold
Builds elite anterior core strength
Teaches rigid core bracing
Carries over to all advanced calisthenics skills
No equipment needed
Develops body control and awareness

description.en: The jack press combines the leg pattern of a jumping jack with an overhead press of light dumbbells (or bodyweight). As you jump your feet wide, you press the dumbbells overhead simultaneously. The combination provides full-body cardio with shoulder loading.

en: Stand tall with feet together and a light dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height.
Jump your feet out to wider than shoulder-width.
Simultaneously press both dumbbells straight up overhead, locking out your arms.
Land softly on the balls of your feet.
Immediately jump your feet back together as you lower the dumbbells back to shoulder height.
Continue alternating between the wide-feet/arms-up and feet-together/arms-down positions.
Move at a brisk, rhythmic pace.
Use light dumbbells (5 to 15 lbs). Perform 30 to 45 seconds per set.
Combines cardio with shoulder loading
Builds shoulder endurance
Excellent total-body conditioning
Time-efficient HIIT exercise
Easy to scale by adjusting dumbbell weight
Engaging variation on jumping jacks

description.en: The kettlebell kickstand one leg deadlift uses a kickstand foot position with one foot forward and the back foot on its toe for balance support. Most of the work falls on the front working leg while the back foot provides light balance. It is a stepping stone between two-leg and full single-leg deadlifts.

en: Hold a kettlebell in your right hand at your side.
Stand with feet hip-width apart.
Step your right foot back into a kickstand position with toe down and heel up.
Most of the work should fall on the left front leg.
Brace your core and lift your chest.
Hinge at the left hip while extending your right leg back slightly.
Lower the kettlebell along the front of your left leg until you feel a strong hamstring stretch.
Drive your left heel into the floor to stand back up. Complete reps, switch sides.
Single-leg bias with kickstand support
Stepping stone to full single-leg RDL
Allows heavier loading than full single-leg version
Strong hamstring and glute development
Useful for progressing single-leg work
Develops hip stability

description.en: The kettlebell unilateral farmers walk is a loaded carry where a heavy kettlebell is held in just one hand. The unilateral load forces the core and obliques to resist lateral flexion while the grip works hard to hold the bell. It builds total-body strength, grip, and core stability.

en: Pick up a heavy kettlebell with one hand.
Stand tall with the bell at your side.
Brace your core hard against the load pulling you sideways.
Keep your shoulders level and your torso vertical.
Walk forward with normal stride length.
Maintain a tight grip on the kettlebell handle.
Walk for the desired distance.
Switch hands and complete reps on the other side.
Builds grip strength
Trains core anti-lateral flexion
Builds total-body strength
Carries over to lifts and sports
Useful for athletes
Strong functional move

description.en: The kneeling single hamstring curl is a single-leg version of the Nordic hamstring curl. The non-working leg is held off the ground while the working leg controls the descent of the body. It is one of the toughest hamstring moves in existence and a serious eccentric strength builder.

en: Kneel on a padded surface and have a partner hold your ankles (or use a fixed anchor).
Lift one leg off the ground behind you.
Brace your core and keep your hips and shoulders aligned.
Use the working hamstring to slowly lower your body forward toward the floor.
Maintain a straight line from knees to head.
Catch yourself with your hands when your strength fails.
Push back up using your hands and the working hamstring.
Complete reps on one side before switching legs.
Brutal eccentric hamstring work
Builds single-leg strength
Reduces hamstring injury risk
Useful for sprinters
Strong unilateral builder
Improves knee flexion strength

description.en: The lying ab press is performed lying on your back with knees bent. By pressing your hands against your bent knees while crunching the shoulders up, you create strong isometric tension on the abs. The push-pull pattern engages the core through resistance against your own body.

en: Lie on your back on the floor.
Bend your knees to 90 degrees with feet off the floor.
Place your palms on the front of your thighs near your knees.
Brace your core and engage your abs.
Press your hands forward against your thighs while your thighs press back into your hands.
At the same time, crunch your shoulders off the floor.
Hold the isometric press for one to two seconds.
Slowly release and lower your shoulders back down.
Strong isometric ab contraction
Builds core endurance
No equipment required
Useful for ab specialization
Easy to scale by changing pressure
Develops mind-muscle connection with abs

description.en: The lying incline hip raise is a reverse crunch performed on a decline bench head down. The lifter lies on the bench gripping the top with both hands, then lifts the hips and legs up. The decline angle increases the load on the lower abs.

en: Set a decline bench with the head lower than the feet.
Lie on the bench with the head at the lower end.
Reach overhead and grip the top of the bench with both hands.
Brace your core hard.
Lift the legs up and curl the hips up off the bench.
Continue until the hips are lifted high and legs are vertical.
Squeeze the lower abs at the top.
Lower the legs and hips back down with control.
Strong lower abs builder
Decline angle adds load
Builds the rectus abdominis
Useful core builder
Strong bench move
Trains hip flexors

description.en: The lever lying single leg curl is performed on a lying leg curl machine with one leg at a time. The single-leg pattern allows focused hamstring training and corrects strength imbalances. The machine fixed path provides constant resistance for hypertrophy-focused training.

en: Position yourself face down on the lying leg curl machine.
Place the back of your right calf against the roller pad.
Grip the handles or the bench for stability.
Brace your core and press your hips into the bench.
Curl your right heel up toward your glute by bending the knee.
Squeeze your right hamstring hard at the top.
Lower the leg back down with control to a fully extended starting position.
Complete reps on one leg, then switch.
Single-leg hamstring isolation
Constant machine resistance
Builds hamstring size and strength
Corrects left-right imbalances
Useful for hypertrophy training
Strong peak contraction

description.en: The lying straight leg marches is a core drill done lying on the back. The mover alternates lifting each straight leg up to ninety degrees in a marching pattern. It builds the lower abs and hip flexors.

en: Lie on the back with the legs straight.
Place the hands at the sides palms down.
Brace your core and keep the lower back on the floor.
Lift one straight leg up toward ninety degrees.
Lower the leg with control to the floor.
Lift the other leg up to ninety degrees.
Continue alternating in a marching pattern.
Keep the motion controlled throughout.
Loads the lower abs
Trains the hip flexors
Strong core drill
No equipment needed
Builds the abs

description.en: The one side archer push up is a unilateral push up variation. The lifter sets the hands wider than shoulder width and bends only one arm during the rep, keeping the other arm straight out to the side. The bent arm carries most of the bodyweight for a brutal unilateral push up.

en: Begin in a high plank position with hands wider than shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core hard.
Lower the body to one side by bending only that arm.
Keep the other arm straight out to the side.
Lower until the chest reaches the bent arm hand.
Press back up using the bent arm to lockout.
Alternate sides each rep.
Brutal unilateral chest builder
Strong push up progression
Builds the chest
Trains shoulder stability
Useful one arm push up prep
Strong calisthenic move

description.en: The prone cobra with palms under thighs places the hands palms down underneath the upper thighs. The position reinforces the back extension and helps activate the upper back as the chest lifts.

en: Lie face down on the floor with the legs extended.
Slide both palms under the upper thighs facing down.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Lift the chest and shoulders off the floor by extending the spine.
Press the palms gently into the thighs to reinforce the lift.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together.
Hold the top position briefly.
Lower the chest back to the floor with control and repeat.
Builds lower back and upper back endurance.
Hand position reinforces the spinal extension.
No equipment needed.
Excellent posture builder.
Reduces upper back stiffness.
Carryover to back squats and deadlifts.

description.en: The resistance band reverse hyper with stability ball on flat bench is a posterior chain drill that uses a stability ball as the support for the hips while a resistance band loaded around the ankles adds resistance during the hyperextension.

en: Place a stability ball on top of a flat bench.
Lie face down with the hips supported on the ball.
Loop a resistance band around both ankles.
Anchor the band end to a low fixed point in front.
Hold the bench for stability.
Brace the core and keep the back flat.
Lift both legs back behind the body against the band.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top then return with control.
Builds the glutes and hamstrings.
Trains the lower back.
Band tension grows through the lift.
Useful posterior chain accessory.
Joint friendly drill.

description.en: The side bridge with bent leg is a regressed side plank. With the bottom knee on the floor, the lever arm is shorter and the demand on the obliques is reduced compared to the full side plank.

en: Lie on your side with the bottom knee bent and the top leg extended.
Place the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder.
Stack the shoulders and hips in line.
Brace the core and squeeze the obliques.
Lift the hips off the floor by pressing the forearm down.
Form a straight line from the head through the top leg.
Hold the position for the desired duration.
Lower the hips and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds oblique and lateral core strength.
Bent knee setup makes the side plank accessible.
No equipment needed.
Excellent foundation for the full side plank.
Carryover to spine stability.
Develops anti lateral flexion strength.

description.en: Side hip abduction is a standing exercise where you lift one leg straight out to the side. It is the same exercise as the standing side leg raise, targeting the gluteus medius and hip abductors for hip stability.

en: Stand tall. Hold a wall for balance.
Shift weight to your left leg.
Lift your right leg straight out to the right side.
Lift to about 30 to 45 degrees.
Keep torso upright.
Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch.
Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Add an ankle weight for progression.
Targets the gluteus medius
Builds hip abductor strength
No equipment needed
Useful for warm-up and rehab
Improves hip stability
Accessible for all levels

description.en: The side lying diagonal backward leg raise is a glute focused drill done lying on the side. Lifting the top leg back and up at a diagonal targets the glute medius and posterior portion of the glute max.

en: Lie on one side on the floor.
Set the bottom leg bent for stability.
Keep the top leg straight.
Rest the head on the bottom arm.
Brace the core and keep the hips stacked.
Lift the top leg back and up at a diagonal angle.
Squeeze the glute hard at the top.
Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Isolates the glute medius.
Trains the outer glute.
Bodyweight move.
Useful for hip stability.
Builds glute size.

description.en: The skip jump rope is a jump-rope variation where you alternate feet with each rope rotation rather than jumping with both feet together. It feels like running in place while jumping rope and is easier to sustain for longer durations than the standard two-foot jump.

en: Hold the jump rope handles with one in each hand. Rope starts behind your feet.
Swing the rope overhead and as it approaches your feet, step over it with your right foot.
On the next rotation, step over with your left foot. Alternate with each swing.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Each hop should be minimal — just enough to clear the rope.
Keep your elbows close to your body. The rotation comes from your wrists, not your shoulders.
Maintain a consistent rhythm. Breathe naturally.
Perform for time (1 to 5 minutes) or rounds.
If the rope catches, reset and continue immediately.
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Easier to sustain than two-foot jumping for longer sessions
Builds calf endurance and ankle stability
Improves coordination and timing
Highly portable — needs only a jump rope
Burns calories at a high rate

description.en: The sledge hammer strike is a full-body conditioning exercise where you swing a sledgehammer overhead and strike a tractor tire repeatedly. It builds explosive rotational power, lat strength, core engagement, and cardiovascular conditioning. It is a staple in strongman and CrossFit training.

en: Stand in front of a tractor tire with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a sledgehammer with both hands, dominant hand near the head, non-dominant hand at the base of the handle.
Lift the sledgehammer overhead. Slide your dominant hand down toward your non-dominant hand as you raise.
At the top, both hands meet at the bottom of the handle.
Drive the sledgehammer down with explosive force, striking the tire.
Use your hips, lats, and core — not just your arms.
The non-dominant hand stays at the base; the dominant hand slides up and down the handle.
Alternate sides — strike right, then left, alternating dominant hand position.
Perform for 30 to 60 seconds per round.
Builds explosive rotational power
Develops lat and core strength
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Trains coordination and timing
Stress-relieving
Used in strongman and CrossFit training

description.en: The smith standing back wrist curl is performed standing with a smith machine bar held behind the back. The wrists curl up and back, isolating the forearm flexors through a small range. The behind-the-back position creates a unique angle that hits the forearms differently than a standard wrist curl.

en: Stand in a smith machine with the bar set behind you at hip height.
Grip the bar behind your back with an underhand grip.
Stand tall with arms straight at your sides.
Brace your core and keep your shoulders pulled back.
Curl the bar up and back by flexing your wrists.
Squeeze the forearms hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Maintain a tall posture throughout.
Builds forearm flexor strength
Unique angle for forearm work
Stable smith machine path
Improves grip strength
Builds forearm size
Useful for forearm variation

description.en: The sprinter crunch is a dynamic core exercise where you lie on your back and explosively sit up while driving one knee toward the opposite elbow, mimicking a sprinting motion. It trains the rectus abdominis, obliques, and hip flexors simultaneously with a dynamic, athletic pattern.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms at your sides and legs extended straight.
Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor.
Explosively sit up while simultaneously driving your right knee toward your chest and swinging your left arm forward (like a sprint).
Your left elbow should approach your right knee. Your right arm swings back naturally.
Pause briefly in the crunch position, then lower back to the flat starting position.
On the next rep, drive your left knee and right arm forward.
Continue alternating for the desired total reps.
Move explosively but with control. Do not slam down on the descent.
Trains the abs, obliques, and hip flexors dynamically
Athletic movement pattern with sports carryover
Builds core power and coordination
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Excellent finisher for core or conditioning workouts
More engaging than static crunches

description.en: The standing lean-back stomach stretch is a simple standing stretch where you place your hands on your lower back and gently arch backward to stretch the abs, hip flexors, and front body. It is one of the simplest counter-stretches for the anterior chain and is excellent after sitting or any flexion-heavy work.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Place both hands on your lower back with fingers pointing down. Use your hands to support and protect your lower back.
Squeeze your glutes. Brace your core.
Slowly lean backward, lifting your chest up toward the ceiling.
Look upward (or keep gaze forward if you have neck issues).
Feel the stretch through your abdominals, chest, and front of the hips.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Slowly return to upright. Repeat 2 to 3 times.
Opens the abs, chest, and hip flexors
Counteracts forward-hunched posture
Quick and accessible
Excellent counter-stretch after core work or sitting
No equipment needed
Improves spinal flexibility

description.en: The suspender chest dip uses suspension straps for a chest-focused dip variation. With the straps held at hip level and the body leaning forward, the press emphasizes the lower chest more than the triceps. The unstable suspension straps add stability work to the standard dip.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about hip height.
Grip both handles with palms facing each other.
Step back to stand between the handles.
Press up to support yourself on the handles with arms extended.
Lean your torso forward at about 30 degrees.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your body by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the starting position by extending the arms.
Bodyweight lower chest emphasis
Strong unstable surface stability work
No bench or dip station required
Builds chest size
Different stimulus than parallel bar dips
Useful for home or travel training

description.en: The suspender single leg split squat is a Bulgarian split squat variation using TRX. The lifter places the rear foot in a TRX foot cradle behind, then performs a split squat. The suspended back foot adds instability and forces strong unilateral leg work.

en: Set the suspension trainer foot cradles at knee height.
Place one foot in the cradle behind you with the laces facing down.
Hop the front foot forward into a long stance.
Brace your core and set the chest tall.
Lower into a split squat by bending the front knee.
Drop the back knee toward the floor.
Drive through the front heel to stand back up.
Lock out and squeeze the front glute. Switch legs and repeat.
Brutal unilateral leg builder
Adds instability to a split squat
Trains balance and stability
Strong TRX move
Builds the glutes
Useful for athletes

description.en: The weighted single leg lift is a leg raise variation done with a dumbbell held between the feet. The lifter lies on the back and lifts each leg one at a time. The added weight loads the hip flexors and lower abs.

en: Lie on the back on a flat bench or floor.
Place a dumbbell between the feet and squeeze it tight.
Brace your core and keep the lower back down.
Place the hands at the sides palms down.
Lift one leg straight up while keeping the other on the floor.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Alternate the working leg each rep.
Loads the lower abs
Trains the hip flexors
Strong weighted variation
Builds the core
Useful ab builder

description.en: The ab wheel run is a dynamic plank variation where you start in a forearm or push-up position with hands on an ab wheel and "walk" forward by alternately pulling the wheel toward you. It combines ab rollout demand with movement, building elite core stability and shoulder endurance.

en: Kneel on the floor with an ab wheel in front of you. Grip the handles with both hands.
Lean forward and assume a plank-like position with your arms extended on the wheel.
Brace your core hard. Maintain a straight body line from knees to hands.
To “run” forward: pull the wheel slightly back toward you with one hand while extending your body forward by walking your knees up.
Continue alternating “wheel-pulling” and small movements to traverse forward.
Move slowly with full core engagement throughout.
Cover the desired distance, then walk the wheel back to start.
This is an advanced exercise — master the standard ab wheel rollout first.
Builds elite core stability under movement
Develops shoulder endurance
Combines rollout demand with cardio
Trains anti-extension under fatigue
Useful advanced core variation
Time-efficient core conditioning
